questions.q: What did King David tell the army?
questions.a: King David told the army that he would also go out with them himself.

questions.q: What was the response from the men in the army to King David?
questions.a: The men told King David not to go out, because he was worth ten thousand of them, and it was better for him to be ready to help them from the city.

questions.q: What instructions did the king give his commanders about Absalom?
questions.a: The king told the commanders not to harm the young man Absalom for his sake.

questions.q: What was the outcome of the battle in the Forest of Ephraim?
questions.a: The people of Israel were struck down before the servants of David, and more of Absalom’s soldiers died because of accidents in the forest than the number of them whom David’s soldiers killed in the battle.

questions.q: What happened to Absalom when the mule he was riding ran under the thick branches of a large oak tree?
questions.a: Absalom’s head was caught in the oak tree. The mule kept going, and that left Absalom dangling in the air.

questions.q: Why was Joab upset with the man who saw Absalom?
questions.a: Joab was upset because the man did not kill Absalom immediately.

questions.q: Why did the man refuse to kill Absalom?
questions.a: He refused because he had heard the king command his commanders to keep from hurting the young man Absalom.

questions.q: What did Joab do to Absalom?
questions.a: Joab took three spears and thrust them into the heart of Absalom while he was still alive in the oak tree.

questions.q: What was done with Absalom’s body?
questions.a: They threw Absalom’s body into a great pit in the forest and set up a very great heap of stones over him.

questions.q: Why had Absalom set up a pillar for himself in the Valley of the King while he was alive?
questions.a: Absalom set up a pillar to make his name remembered, because he said he had no son to make people remember his name.

questions.q: Why did Joab tell Ahimaaz not to run to the king with the news?
questions.a: Joab told him not to bring the news that day because the king’s son was dead.

questions.q: Why did Ahimaaz still run and tell David the news?
questions.a: Ahimaaz insisted on running after the Cushite, even though Joab told him there was no reward for the news, so Joab told him to go.

questions.q: What did the king think when the watcher reported a lone runner?
questions.a: The king said that if the man was by himself, that indicates that he is bringing news.

questions.q: What did the king think when the watcher reported another lone runner?
questions.a: The king said that this one was also bringing news.

questions.q: What did the king think when the watcher identified the first runner as Ahimaaz?
questions.a: The king said that he was a good man and came with good news.

questions.q: What news did Ahimaaz bring to the king?
questions.a: Ahimaaz told the king that Yahweh had defeated the men who had lifted their hand against the king.

questions.q: How did Ahimaaz answer when the king asked about Absalom?
questions.a: Ahimaaz said he saw a great tumult but did not know what it was about.

questions.q: What was the Cushite’s answer when the king asked about Absalom?
questions.a: The Cushite said that he wished that what happened to Absalom would happen to all of David’s enemies and to anyone who rebels against him.

questions.q: How did the king respond to the news of his son’s death?
questions.a: The king trembled, went up to the upper room of the gate, and wept, wishing he had died in place of his son.

commentary.text: Verses 1–8 How does David render good for evil! Absalom would have only David smitten; David would have only Absalom spared. This seems to be a resemblance of man's wickedness towards God, and God's mercy to man, of which it is hard to say which is most amazing. Now the Israelites see what it is to take counsel against the Lord and his anointed.

Let young people look upon Absalom, hanging on a tree, accursed, forsaken of heaven and earth; there let them read the Lord's abhorrence of rebellion against parents. Nothing can preserve men from misery and contempt, but heavenly wisdom and the grace of God.

By directing David to give God thanks for his victory, Ahimaaz prepared him for the news of his son's death. The more our hearts are fixed and enlarged, in thanksgiving to God for our mercies, the better disposed we shall be to bear with patience the afflictions mixed with them. Some think David's wish arose from concern about Absalom's everlasting state; but he rather seems to have spoken without due thought. He is to be blamed for showing so great fondness for a graceless son. Also for quarrelling with Divine justice. And for opposing the justice of the nation, which, as king, he had to administer, and which ought to be preferred before natural affection. The best men are not always in a good frame; we are apt to over-grieve for what we over-loved. But while we learn from this example to watch and pray against sinful indulgence, or neglect of our children, may we not, in David, perceive a shadow of the Saviour's love, who wept over, prayed for, and even suffered death for mankind, though vile rebels and enemies.
